commenti.body: The funny thing is that I enjoyed both Megalopolis and Cats a lot. I would much rather watch a weird and ambitious failure than a film with no ambition or one made for the masses. I think Megalopolis is legitimately great but you need to take it on its own terms, it's a bonkers and vibey film

Yeah I think OP is missing the very large point here. I had an absolute blast the entire time watching Megalopolis due to how strange it was. It felt like I was experiencing a piece of history. 120 million self financed film is so wild and ambitious and interesting. I would rather Megalopolis than a marvel movie any day. I wouldn't call it a good movie though, just a very very enjoyable experience with some hilarious moments and memorable performances.
I don’t love MCU films, but women tend to not be terrorized on their sets.

It had bow-and-arrow boners, the cure to being shot point-blank in the face, Auntie Wow, and a wonderful “The The” credits song. It’s definitely messy and ridiculous at every single turn but I can’t dislike something so earnest and ambitious. I simply don’t have the capacity for such hate. Megalopolis and Southland Tales would be a beautifully brain-bending double feature of crazy, dumb, and inspired big swings. Long live the Megalon!

There is a difference between the film and the process of making the film. I obviously don't support that, but I think a film should be judged on its own merits. If I judged films based on every bad thing that happened on set, a lot of great films would fall under that category. Also, are you even sure that MCU films don't have issues with the production?

Truly baffling how people are talking about this movie. Some of the most original, daring and inventive editing and insane directing choices. It confuses me a lot because a lot of people who argue that they’re tired of franchises or the same copy-paste machine that spits out stuff like Free Guy can look at this messy, maximalist fantasy of a guy who has a ridiculous amount of money to do as he pleases, I mean isn’t that what we kind of want from our favorite directors? Being able to follow an idea all the way through (you can argue about the messiness and the incongruence all you want but this movie is trying to at least *do something*) and come out the other end with something that imprints something on you? 

I just do not get what you all want out of filmmaking at this point. You guys want boldness, risk and originality but when it comes to you because it doesn’t check off all the plot-boxes you want and because some characters are kooky (God forbid) you have to flame it and even start to yearn for the baby food franchises you mentioned at the beginning of your post. Do you want perfection? Well it’s not there and if you’re looking for it in art bring a book. You don’t think the man who made Godfather and Apocalypse Now doesn’t know what would please everyone? Come on man. What are we doing here?

I think that’s an incredibly unfair double standard that is being applied here isn’t it?

The OP is praising the film for being self-financed. And it’s just hard for me to Quixotic charm to a film from a director who championed his “anti-woke” film, hired “cancelled” actors, and terrorized women, straight up kissing a child.    

My point is that it being a self-financed auteur experience isn’t a reason to praise the film especially considering the on set conditions.

That's fair and your original comment wasn't in response to me directly, but two things I'd say to counter it:

1. I think the film holds up as interesting and weird in its own right regardless of how it was financed
2. The fact it was financed by selling his vineyard is all part of the narrative about how FFC has always wanted to make this film but never been able to. Knowing that this is something he's been obsessed with, that it's a labour of love and passion project helps to understand where it's coming from. The stuff you're talking about has no bearing on that, it's just some shitty things that happened.

I do agree that the "anti-woke" stuff is total bullshit, mind. The fact I hate Shia made it easier to hate him in the film but I don't think that's enough to justify supporting his career

I appreciate this review very much. 

My personal reaction, having *just* seen it, is pretty aligned with the "this is an interesting mess" crowd, and I did find it refreshing in some ways. On the other hand, I think we need to get past the idea of just saying, "it's an idiosyncratic vision" and "the movie takes big swings". I appreciate that, but if we want to take the movie seriously, we've got to actually \_look\_ at the vision and swings at some point. So I appreciate you doing that.

I wasn't bothered by the episodic nature. Some of the reason you (and others) hate it is that the movie pretty heavily flirts with the idea of killing thousands of people to usher in the better world, most notable in the treatment of the satellite crash. But the movie wants it both ways: later on, it's very important that every family has its own garden. Very Fountainhead, but handled with more clarity and depth there(!). 

I think your critique of the Megalon is spot on. Since it can do anything one wants and can only be deployed by the protagonist, there's no stakes or drama. I suppose there could have been, if the movie wanted to take the romance seriously, but Julia's character's underdevelopment seems like a problem for that subplot.

Reflecting a little more on it, maybe part of the problem is that it's not really a "singular" vision (I don't mean, necessarily, a single person's vision, but rather a vision that has some kind of coherence and integrity). It may have been, at one point, but I wonder if a lot of FFC's ideas got discarded, and he hoped something emerged from the collaboration.

The whole discourse surrounding this movie is pretty baffling to me. And this OP's review is no different. I simply cannot understand how a movie, especially one like this could possibly make you angry in a way that you claim that "maybe we should go back to the franchises"

I watched probably like thousands of movies, some of them i liked, some of them i hated to my guts, but i was never *angry* and frustrated with a movie. Even at their lowest, movies are just - bad. Boring. Slog. Whatever adjective you want to use. But never anger-inducing.

Speaking of megalopolis, i also cant understand why there were so many reviews using exact same words as OP - that it made them angry. Or calling it "one of the worst movies ive ever watched". I totally understand if someone hates it. If someone thinks its bad. If its not everyones cup of tea. And frankly, probably it isnt the greatest movie ever made. But in my opinion, its a far cry from "worst movie ever", as its being labeled almost in unison. It is bold and innocative. Its original. Its also cliché and messy for the most part. But nevertheless, it is also (for me) captivating and interesting, and one of the better movie experiences of the year.

I really want to know what the opinion of it will be in 30-40 years, after the dust is settled. I dont think it will go in history as a masterpiece and one of the greatest movies ever (though i personally enjoyed it). But i also dont think it will be remembered as the opposite thing, as the worst movie ever, prevailing opinion since the release. What i guess is, some 30-40 years from now movie will be looked as a bold but average conclusion to one of cinemas finest directors. Certainly not the worst movie ever.

I watched it last night. Cannot relate to your reaction at all. It was very clear from the beginning that it is tongue-in-cheek. It gives you permission to laugh at it- and when you do, apparently you think you've caught Coppola making a fool of himself? It's a silly, fun, playful movie. What's there to be angry about? Why not just relax and have fun?

> now movie will be looked as a bold but average conclusion to one of cinemas finest directors. Certainly not the worst movie ever.

He’s making another film
